Countable vs Uncountable

See the rationals numbered in a single list. Then see the same attempt fail for the reals.

Countable means pairing off with the natural numbers. Fractions tile a grid, and a zigzag count numbers them all. Reals refuse. Every proposed list misses some real. Changing digits along the diagonal proves it.

For example, hand number tickets to every 🧑 classmate. However long the line, one ticket each means countable. If every roster still misses someone, the crowd cannot be counted.

Prove (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) is uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument.

dn={5rn’s nth digit≠56otherwise(dn is the nth digit of x)d_n = \begin{cases} 5 & r_n\text{'s }n\text{th digit} \ne 5 \\ 6 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad (d_n \text{ is the } n\text{th digit of } x)dn​={56​rn​’s nth digit=5otherwise​(dn​ is the nth digit of x)
Show proof

  1. Suppose the elements of (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) could be fully enumerated as r1,r2,…r_1, r_2, \dotsr1​,r2​,…. Each rnr_nrn​ has a unique decimal expansion not ending in infinite 999s, so its nnn-th digit is well defined.

  2. Define the nnn-th digit dnd_ndn​ of xxx to be 555 when rnr_nrn​'s nnn-th digit is not 555, and 666 otherwise.

    Then x∈(0,1)x \in (0,1)x∈(0,1).

    To pass from a digit difference to x≠rnx \ne r_nx=rn​ the dual-expansion issue must be addressed: the expansion of xxx uses only the digits 555 and 666, so it has no tail of 000s and no tail of 999s.

    But two decimal expansions of the same number are possible only when one ends in a tail of 000s and the other in a tail of 999s, so an expansion using only 5,65, 65,6 is the unique — canonical — expansion of xxx.

    It differs from the canonical expansion of rnr_nrn​ at digit nnn, hence x≠rnx \ne r_nx=rn​ for every nnn — a contradiction.

  3. Hence no enumeration of (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) exists: (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) is uncountable.
